prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: After reading the eight opening ballots I move my first choice from B048 to B047. The optical lattice clock is a new measurement capability that has been reproduced and improved by many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE), with intercomparisons agreeing near 1e-18. The credited pair is clean: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first strontium lattice clocks, and Jun Ye brought accuracy, stability and many-body control to the record level. It has five of eight members ranking it, two of them first, and every ballot that names laureates agrees on the same two people, which is rare on this shortlist. As a detector builder I value work where calibration and systematics were done patiently enough that the community believes the number, and here they were. The physics also reaches beyond metrology: relativistic redshift across millimetres, tests of constant variation, dark-matter searches and the pending redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the fundamental-physics payoff so far is limits, not discoveries, and a prize for precision metrology can look like a sequel to the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. The redefinition of the second has not happened yet, so the most visible consequence is still ahead. A second reservation is that B047 sits at rank 6 or 7 for two colleagues and so does not command the broadest support: B006 was ranked by seven members and sits in the top three of four. If the committee wants the widest consensus rather than the cleanest credit, B006 is the better fit, at the cost of the four-names-into-three problem.

responses.point: Topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect are a clean conceptual advance: a sharp prediction, a decisive transport experiment, about twenty years of confirmation across materials, with timing that is ripe.
responses.response: I agree on the science and ranked B006 fourth myself, and I accept your maturity argument fully. My difficulty is attribution, and the opening ballots show it: four of seven proposals take Hasan with Kane and Molenkamp, and two take Mele instead. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted HgTe, and Zhang is deceased, so the story of who was decisive is more contested than for the clock. Also, I am not an expert on condensed matter, so I will not claim your topological argument is wrong. I therefore keep B006 as my first alternative, not my preferred option, until the committee settles who the third name is.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks reached roughly 1e-18 through magic-wavelength trapping, are reproduced by many laboratories, and a two-person prize for Katori and Ye is natural, with timing helped by the coming redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree, and your point about independent laboratories is why I treat this as settled measurement and not a single-group claim. I would qualify one thing you flag: the earlier Hall and Hänsch comb prize and Wineland's 2012 prize mean the citation must be written around the lattice-clock concept and its accuracy, not generic precision spectroscopy. I would ask you, as the atomic physicist here, whether the many-body, Fermi-degenerate clock results alone make the Ye credit distinct from the comb prize, or whether the redefinition of the second is the real test.

responses.point: Circuit QED is the enabling platform for microwave quantum optics and superconducting qubits, reproduced for twenty years, with a natural Blais-Wallraff-Schoelkopf trio; the clock ranks sixth.
responses.response: I take the platform argument seriously, and B038 is a very successful field. My serious concern is the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which Kroll, Mehlig and Olsson also mention. Granting another superconducting-circuit prize one year later seems hard to defend when Girvin and Huang are missing from the credit and Devoret is already a laureate. I would put B038 behind the clock for now, and I would like your view on whether the credit is robust without Girvin.

responses.point: Baryon acoustic oscillations are a clean standard ruler and a cornerstone of the dark-energy measurement, confirmed by SDSS, 2dFGRS and later BOSS and DESI.
responses.response: I share the instrumental respect for BAO, having ranked it fifth, and the independent detection by two surveys is a strong point. What keeps it below the clock for me is that the names do not map onto the achievement: the theoretical originators are not on the list, survey leadership was broad, and the prize would lean on a large collaboration. I am also unsure that BAO is distinct from the 2011 and 2019 cosmology prizes in the committee's eyes. I would be glad to hear whether you think a clean three-name credit exists.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers B006, with the widest ballot support but an unresolved third name (Hasan or Mele), over B047, with narrower support but a clean credit.
Whether the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes make a lattice-clock prize look incremental, and whether the redefinition of the second should come first.
Whether B048 (IceCube) can be credited to two individuals fairly given AMANDA, DUMAND and the large collaboration; I have reduced my own ranking of it because of this and the thin support.
I cannot independently assess the condensed-matter credit disputes (B006, B017) and rely on colleagues and expert reviewers.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B047, B006 or B048. My PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations are not connected to the lattice clock, topological insulators or IceCube, though IceCube (B048) is in my own astroparticle field, and I disclose that closeness for the record as I rank it as an alternative.
